She was born on June 21,1929 to Lars and Borghild Brekke and grew up on a farm near Deerfield and graduated from Deerfield High School. Audrey and Bob were married for 60 years. After his passing, she developed a close friendship with Keith Simmons and they had many wonderful times and travels together. Justia Opinion Summary

James Albert Trankle created two entities, including “Good Charity Church Inc.” and “Restaurant Buyers Club Society,” and collected over $200,000 through mail solicitations using trade names similar to those of legitimate charities. The solicitations often misled donors about the true nature of the organizations and the use of donated funds, which were largely spent on personal expenses by Trankle and his associate, Stephen Sibert. Unlike the legitimate “Good Charity Inc.,” which was a registered 501(c)(3) organization, Trankle’s entities were not bona fide charities and did not properly use or report donations.
A federal grand jury in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia indicted Trankle on ten counts, including conspiracy to commit mail and bank fraud, bank fraud, and aggravated identity theft. Prior to trial, several counts of aggravated identity theft were dismissed. At trial, the jury convicted Trankle on six counts: conspiracy to commit mail and bank fraud and five counts of bank fraud. Trankle’s post-trial motions for judgment of acquittal or a new trial were denied. The court then sentenced him to 60 months imprisonment and ordered forfeiture and restitution based on the proceeds of his fraudulent scheme.

# USA v. Trankle, 23-3233 (D.C. Cir. 2026)
James Albert Trankle created two entities, including “Good Charity Church Inc.” and “Restaurant Buyers Club Society,” and collected over $200,000 through mail solicitations using trade names similar to those of legitimate charities. The solicitations often misled donors about the true nature of the organizations and the use of donated funds, which were largely spent on personal expenses by Trankle and his associate, Stephen Sibert. Unlike the legitimate “Good Charity Inc.,” which was a registered 501(c)(3) organization, Trankle’s entities were not bona fide charities and did not properly use or report donations.  
A federal grand jury in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia indicted Trankle on ten counts, including conspiracy to commit mail and bank fraud, bank fraud, and aggravated identity theft. Prior to trial, several counts of aggravated identity theft were dismissed. At trial, the jury convicted Trankle on six counts: conspiracy to commit mail and bank fraud and five counts of bank fraud. Trankle’s post-trial motions for judgment of acquittal or a new trial were denied. The court then sentenced him to 60 months imprisonment and ordered forfeiture and restitution based on the proceeds of his fraudulent scheme.
The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reviewed Trankle’s appeals regarding evidentiary rulings, sufficiency of the evidence, and sentencing. The court held that the district court properly excluded certain documents as hearsay and found no abuse of discretion or reversible error. The evidence at trial was sufficient for a reasonable jury to convict Trankle. The district court’s application of sentencing enhancements and calculation of forfeiture were affirmed, as was Trankle’s sentence. The judgment and challenged rulings of the district court were affirmed in full.

The solicitations often misled donors about the true nature of the organizations and the use of donated funds, which were largely spent on personal expenses by Trankle and his associate, Stephen Sibert.
Unlike the legitimate “Good Charity Inc.,” which was a registered 501(c)(3) organization, Trankle’s entities were not bona fide charities and did not properly use or report donations.
A federal grand jury in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia indicted Trankle on ten counts, including conspiracy to commit mail and bank fraud, bank fraud, and aggravated identity theft.
...
At trial, the jury convicted Trankle on six counts: conspiracy to commit mail and bank fraud and five counts of bank fraud.
...
The court then sentenced him to 60 months imprisonment and ordered forfeiture and restitution based on the proceeds of his fraudulent scheme.
The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reviewed Trankle’s appeals regarding evidentiary rulings, sufficiency of the evidence, and sentencing.
The court held that the district court properly excluded certain documents as hearsay and found no abuse of discretion or reversible error.
The evidence at trial was sufficient for a reasonable jury to convict Trankle.
The district court’s application of sentencing enhancements and calculation of forfeiture were affirmed, as was Trankle’s sentence.

webiq.title: United States v. Trankle — D.C. Circuit upheld charity-fraud convictions, sentence, and forfeiture order – Case Law Wire
webiq.snippet:
A jury convicted Trankle of conspiracy to commit mail and bank fraud and five substantive counts of bank fraud. The district court denied his motions for acquittal or a new trial, applied enhancements for his leadership role, misrepresenting that he acted for a charitable organization, and using sophisticated means, and sentenced him to 60 months in prison. It also ordered $158,709 in restitution and $135,327 in forfeiture. ... The D.C. Circuit affirmed. It held that Trankle adequately preserved his evidentiary challenge but that the district court did not abuse its discretion by treating the writings as hearsay offered to prove Trankle’s asserted purpose. Trankle also failed to establish that the writings reflected his then-existing state of mind as required by Federal Rule of Evidence 803 (3), because the record did not show when the statements were made. Although the district court erred by restricting defense counsel’s opportunity to explain the asserted exception, that error was harmless because comparable evidence was admitted or available for cross-examination.

The court also held that sufficient evidence supported the jury’s finding of fraudulent intent, including false representations about the organizations, the use of donations, and authorization for recurring payments. It upheld all three sentencing enhancements and found the within-Guidelines 60-month sentence procedurally and substantively reasonable.

Finally, the court upheld the $135,327 forfeiture order. Although forfeiture generally reaches property a defendant actually acquired, proceeds generated through activities directly supervised by an organization’s leader may be attributed to that leader. Because Trankle led the conspiracy, supervised Sibert, and participated in the operations producing the proceeds, the district court properly held him responsible for the amount deposited into the entities’ accounts.
